human_review.instructions: Validate all claims in this report against the references provided, then review, edit, and approve its contents. Set approved to true once done.

stages.stage_name: Open Input Data and Measurement Evidence
stages.score_derivation: There is moderate but incomplete public evidence for input-data traceability. The README identifies that GFW map layers and datasets are stored in the Resource Watch API and gives a concrete endpoint for GFW-specific datasets, while the API documentation explains dataset, layer, vocabulary, and metadata fields used by the front end. Some calculation documentation names specific input columns and a Geotrellis table identifier for above-ground biomass. However, the evidence bundle does not include the actual dataset metadata records, primary dataset provenance, measurement protocols, uncertainty estimates, quality controls, data licences, versioning of datasets, or traceability from secondary products back to primary measurements. The score is therefore above fragmentary because inputs are at least identifiable through APIs and metadata conventions, but not higher because core measurement evidence and reusable/versioned data provenance are not shown.
stages.uncertainty_reason: The repository documents where data are referenced, but the bundle does not include the external API records or underlying datasets needed to verify provenance and quality.

references.label: README data/API reference
references.quote_or_finding: Map layers and relevant datasets are stored in the RW-API, and the README gives the endpoint `https://api.resourcewatch.org/v1/dataset?app=gfw&includes=layer,vocabulary,metadata&page[size]=200`.
references.relevance: Shows that relevant input datasets are identifiable through a public API and that the web app uses external dataset/layer records.

references.label: GFW API documentation
references.quote_or_finding: Documents GFW dataset syntax, vocabulary tags, metadata fields, layer configuration, ISO applicability, legend configuration, and external `moreInfo` links.
references.relevance: Supports partial documentation of data-layer metadata and transformations used by the application.

references.label: Climate widget calculations
references.quote_or_finding: Identifies above-ground biomass as coming from the `whrc_aboveground_biomass_stock_2000__Mg` column within summary Geotrellis tables, including table `998dd97a-389f-4a02-988f-17b184f507ac`.
references.relevance: Provides a concrete example of an input field and table used in a derived environmental calculation.

stages.score_derivation: The software is publicly available in a version-controlled GitHub repository under the MIT licence, and the README provides basic technology, installation, development, deployment, and release information. The repository includes documentation of several analytical methods used in widgets, including formulas for biomass/carbon conversions and statistical bands. CI workflows and CodeQL configuration are public. This is strong evidence for open-source front-end software and some open analytical logic. The score is not higher because the bundle does not include dependency manifests, full environment configuration, backend/API source code, data-processing pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, or complete model implementations for the broader Global Forest Watch evidence system. The repository appears to contain the web app rather than all data-generation and environmental modelling components.
stages.uncertainty_reason: The front-end codebase and licence are clear, but the evidence does not cover all software and models needed to produce GFW environmental claims.

references.label: Repository metadata
references.quote_or_finding: Repository description: “Global Forest Watch: An online, global, near-real time forest monitoring tool”; licence listed as MIT; default branch `develop`; topics include deforestation, forest-monitoring, satellite-imagery, Next.js, React, Redux.
references.relevance: Establishes that the project software is public, version-controlled, and openly licensed.

references.label: MIT licence
references.quote_or_finding: The licence grants permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and sell copies of the software, subject to MIT terms.
references.relevance: Supports open-source reuse rights for the repository software.

references.label: README installation and architecture
references.quote_or_finding: The app is built with Next.js, React, and Redux; installation steps include cloning the repo, running `yarn`, copying `.env.sample` to `.env.local`, and starting with `yarn dev`.
references.relevance: Shows public documentation of software stack and basic runnable setup.

references.label: Widget calculation documentation
references.quote_or_finding: Documents mathematical/statistical calculations for dashboard widgets, including mean, standard deviation, zero-filling, ISO week grouping, and temporal smoothing.
references.relevance: Shows that some analytical methods behind displayed indicators are publicly inspectable.

stages.score_derivation: There is moderate evidence that the web application can be installed, run locally, linted, tested, and deployed in a repeatable way. The README gives development commands and describes staging, pre-production, production, and review-app deployment flows. GitHub Actions define CI on pull requests and pushes, including Node.js version 18.15.0, dependency installation, linting, and unit tests. However, this evidence mainly supports reproducibility of the front-end application, not reproducibility of environmental outputs. The bundle does not include exact workflow runs connecting particular input datasets to published claims, pinned dataset versions, model parameters, output snapshots, computational notebooks, workflow orchestration files, or re-executable end-to-end data pipelines. The score is therefore moderate but limited.
stages.uncertainty_reason: Execution evidence is clear for software CI and development, but missing for end-to-end environmental computations and reported outputs.

references.label: README local execution
references.quote_or_finding: Getting-started instructions: clone the repository, install dependencies with `yarn`, copy `.env.sample` to `.env.local`, and run `yarn dev` to access the app on port 3000.
references.relevance: Provides basic public instructions for reproducing the application runtime locally.

references.label: README deployment workflow
references.quote_or_finding: Pull requests merge into `develop`, which deploys to staging and pre-production; `master` deploys automatically to production; Heroku review apps are created for pull requests.
references.relevance: Shows an inspectable development/deployment process, though not an environmental computation run record.

references.label: CI workflow
references.quote_or_finding: CI runs on pull requests to develop/master and pushes to master/develop; jobs use Ubuntu, Node 18.15.0, `yarn`, `yarn lint`, and `yarn test:ci`.
references.relevance: Supports reproducibility of software checks and test execution in a standard environment.

stages.score_derivation: There is moderate evidence of open software review mechanisms. The GitHub repository has a public issue count, uses pull requests, CI, review apps, and CodeQL analysis, which supports visible bug reporting and code scrutiny. The README describes a Gitflow workflow and automatic review apps for pull requests. However, the evidence bundle does not include actual issue discussions, pull request review records, governance documents, public methodological debates, peer review, correction notices, replication attempts, affected-community engagement, or records showing how environmental claims were challenged and improved. The score is not lower because open GitHub workflows and issue tracking are present, but not higher because review traceability for the underlying environmental evidence and claims is not demonstrated.
stages.uncertainty_reason: The bundle confirms open software-review infrastructure but not the substance or quality of community and scientific review.

runs.single_paragraph_summary: The wri/gfw repository provides strong open-source evidence for the Global Forest Watch web application, including a public MIT-licensed codebase, installation instructions, CI workflows, deployment practices, and documentation of some widget calculations and API metadata conventions. It also provides partial traceability to input data through the Resource Watch API endpoint and examples of columns/tables used in calculations. However, the supplied evidence mainly covers the front-end application and selected calculation documentation, not the full environmental evidence chain behind specific Global Forest Watch claims. Key gaps include primary data provenance, measurement methods, uncertainty and quality-control records, dataset licences and versions, backend/data-processing pipelines, exact reproducible workflow runs, claim-specific output snapshots, publication licences, review records, and explicit versioned linkage from claims to data, code, execution, review, and publication artifacts.
limitations: The evidence bundle contains repository metadata and selected files only; it does not include the actual Resource Watch API dataset records returned by the documented endpoint.
No specific environmental claim, dashboard indicator page, report, or output snapshot was supplied, so claim-level traceability could not be assessed directly.

The repository appears to be primarily the GFW web app; backend services, data-processing pipelines, remote-sensing workflows, and dataset production systems may exist elsewhere but are not evidenced here.
Dependency manifests, `.env.sample`, test results, release pages, pull request discussions, issue contents, and GitHub Actions run logs were not included in the evidence bundle.
No primary measurement evidence, uncertainty estimates, quality-control documentation, dataset version history, or data-use licences were supplied for the environmental datasets.
No peer-review records, correction notices, public methodological discussions, governance records, or replication attempts were included.

runs.single_paragraph_summary: Global Forest Watch’s public `wri/gfw` repository provides a relatively strong open-source front-end and useful public documentation for dataset/layer schemas, deployment, releases, and several widget calculations, with an MIT licence, CI, CodeQL, and local run instructions. Its strongest traceability dimensions are open-source software/methods and public communication, while execution reproducibility is only moderate because the exact environmental data-processing runs, input snapshots, parameters, and output artifacts are not supplied. Input-data traceability is partial: the repository points to the Resource Watch API and names some fields/tables, but does not expose primary measurement provenance, uncertainties, dataset licences, or quality controls in the bundle. Community/review evidence shows public GitHub mechanisms and automated checks but not substantive review records. Open linkage is the main weakness: there are pointers among app, API, metadata, formulas, and releases, but no explicit, versioned, externally verifiable chain from a specific environmental claim to exact datasets, code version, workflow run, review record, and publication.
limitations: The assessment uses only the supplied evidence bundle and does not inspect the live Global Forest Watch website, Resource Watch API responses, GitHub issues, pull requests, releases, or source files not included in the bundle.

The bundle primarily documents the web app, not the upstream data pipelines, primary satellite/field measurements, backend APIs, Geotrellis tables, or data-processing infrastructure that produce many environmental outputs.
No specific environmental claim or dashboard value was supplied, so claim-level traceability could not be tested directly.

Dataset licences, primary data provenance, measurement methods, uncertainty/error estimates, quality-control procedures, and dataset version histories were not included for the underlying forest-monitoring inputs.
The evidence includes review infrastructure but not actual review discussions, peer-review reports, correction notices, governance records, or affected-community feedback.

The evidence does not include immutable workflow run IDs, output artifacts, exact API snapshots, environment variable examples, dependency lockfiles, or deployment logs needed for stronger reproducibility and linkage scoring.

runs.single_paragraph_summary: Global Forest Watch’s public web-app repository provides substantial open-source software evidence: an MIT license, documented installation and deployment workflow, CI/CodeQL automation, API schema documentation, and some open documentation of widget calculations. It also points to the Resource Watch API as the source of map layers and datasets and gives a few concrete input references, such as a biomass column and Geotrellis table UUID. However, the supplied evidence is primarily for the front-end application and its configuration rather than for the full environmental evidence chain. It does not include the underlying primary datasets, dataset versions, measurement methods, uncertainty and quality-control documentation, complete reproducible data-processing workflows, exact claim-to-data/code/run links, substantive public review records, or versioned publication artifacts. As a result, the project scores strongly for open-source software, moderately for execution, communication, input-data traceability, and community review, and weaker for explicit claim-level linkage.

references.label: Widget calculation documentation
references.quote_or_finding: The document gives mathematical formulas and preparation steps for statistical bands in Fires and GLAD widgets, including weekly aggregation, zero-filling, means, standard deviations, and smoothing.
references.relevance: Shows that at least some analytical methods behind displayed indicators are publicly documented.

stages.score_derivation: There is moderate evidence for reproducible software execution of the web app: the README provides local installation and development commands, describes deployment branches and environments, and the repository includes CI workflows for linting, unit tests, and CodeQL analysis on pull requests and pushes. These practices make the application build and quality-check process partly inspectable. The score is not higher because the supplied evidence does not include a captured or versioned workflow run connecting specific environmental input datasets to specific displayed outputs, pinned data snapshots, full environment files, backend/API execution instructions, or re-executable notebooks/pipelines for the environmental calculations. External users can likely run the front end, but cannot from the bundle reproduce an exact GFW environmental claim end-to-end.
stages.uncertainty_reason: The repository contains clear app execution and CI evidence, but end-to-end claim reproduction depends on external APIs and data not included in the evidence bundle.

references.label: README local execution instructions
references.quote_or_finding: The README instructs users to clone the repo, run yarn, copy .env.sample to .env.local, and start the server with yarn dev at http://0.0.0.0:3000.
references.relevance: Supports reproducibility of the web application execution environment at a basic level.

references.label: README deployment workflow
references.quote_or_finding: The README describes Gitflow deployment: develop to staging/pre-production, master to production, Heroku review apps for pull requests, and NEXT_PUBLIC_FEATURE_ENV to select environments.
references.relevance: Provides public information on execution/deployment pathways, though not exact environmental computation runs.

references.label: CI workflow
references.quote_or_finding: The workflow runs on pull requests and pushes to develop/master, sets Node 18.15.0, installs modules with yarn, runs ESLint, and runs unit tests with yarn test:ci.
references.relevance: Shows automated, inspectable execution checks for the codebase.

references.label: CodeQL workflow
references.quote_or_finding: The CodeQL workflow runs JavaScript analysis on push, pull_request, and a weekly schedule.
references.relevance: Adds evidence of automated reproducible security/static analysis, though not environmental result reproduction.

stages.score_derivation: There is partial evidence of open review and correction channels. The public GitHub repository has open issues, uses pull requests against develop/master, runs CI on pull requests, and creates Heroku review apps for pull requests; the README also describes releases and semantic changelog practices. These mechanisms make some software review and change processes visible. The score is not higher because the evidence bundle does not include specific issue discussions, pull-request reviews, governance records, peer review, public methodological debates, correction notices, affected-community feedback processes, or responses to challenges about environmental claims. The evidence supports ordinary open-source software review more than full open scientific/community review of the claims and datasets.
stages.uncertainty_reason: Open issue and pull-request mechanisms are evident, but the supplied artifacts do not show the substance or quality of review around environmental claims.

references.label: Repository metadata open issues
references.quote_or_finding: The metadata reports open_issues_count: 16.
references.relevance: Indicates a public issue tracker exists, though the evidence bundle does not show issue contents or responses.

references.label: README pull request and review app process
references.quote_or_finding: The README says pull requests are merged into develop, Heroku Review Apps are created automatically when a pull request is opened, and a link is added to the pull request.
references.relevance: Shows visible mechanisms for reviewing proposed software changes.

references.label: CI on pull requests
references.quote_or_finding: The CI workflow runs linting and unit tests on pull requests to develop and master, except unit tests are skipped for draft pull requests.
references.relevance: Supports automated review/quality control during contribution review.

references.label: README release process
references.quote_or_finding: The README says GitHub releases are used to record changes to the app and describes semantic release tagging and changelog generation.
references.relevance: Shows some public change-record practice, but not necessarily claim correction or scientific review.

stages.score_derivation: The project has reasonably strong public communication for a web dashboard: the repository describes Global Forest Watch as a dynamic online forest monitoring and alert system, links to the public website, documents setup and data-layer conventions, and provides calculation documents for climate and alert widgets. These materials help external users understand at least some claims, indicators, and methods. The score is not higher because the supplied evidence does not include specific published reports or papers, dashboard version history, data update-cycle documentation, content licences such as Creative Commons for publications, formal review status, or explicit citations from outputs to exact supporting artifacts. Communication is open and useful, but incomplete for full publication traceability of environmental claims.
stages.uncertainty_reason: The bundle includes public dashboard and documentation evidence but not the full set of publications, update histories, or licensing/review information for communicated outputs.

references.label: README public GFW description
references.quote_or_finding: The README states that Global Forest Watch is a dynamic online forest monitoring and alert system and links to http://www.globalforestwatch.org/.
references.relevance: Shows the public communication/output channel and the broad environmental monitoring claim.

references.label: API documentation for dashboard layers
references.quote_or_finding: The API documentation explains how datasets and layers are represented in the application, including metadata used in slide-out tabs and legends.
references.relevance: Supports interpretability of dashboard outputs and indicators.

references.label: Climate widget calculations
references.quote_or_finding: The document explains formulas for below-ground biomass, total biomass, carbon stock, below-ground carbon, and total carbon stock calculations.
references.relevance: Provides explanatory material for users scrutinizing climate/carbon widget outputs.

references.label: Widget calculation documentation
references.quote_or_finding: The document outlines mathematical and statistical calculations used in dashboard widgets, including GLAD and Fires seasonal and cumulative widgets.
references.relevance: Supports open communication of methods behind some dynamic dashboard outputs.

stages.score_derivation: The project provides some linkage across the evidence chain: the README links the web app to the Resource Watch API dataset endpoint; API documentation explains how dataset metadata keys, layers, legends, and external links are used; and calculation docs connect certain widget formulas to named columns and a table UUID. This is enough to show partial linkages between app outputs, API datasets, and documented methods. However, linkage is not explicit or versioned enough for high traceability. The evidence bundle does not provide claim-level links from a specific dashboard value to exact dataset versions, primary measurements, code commits, API records, model parameters, workflow runs, review records, or publication versions. It also does not show persistent identifiers or provenance records tying all six dimensions together. Therefore the evidence chain is only partially inspectable and remains below the moderate-to-strong threshold.
stages.uncertainty_reason: Some cross-links between app, API datasets, metadata, and methods are documented, but exact versioned claim-to-evidence chains are absent from the supplied evidence.

references.label: README app-to-API linkage
references.quote_or_finding: The README states that map layers and relevant datasets are stored in the RW-API and that globalforestwatch.org/map uses layer-manager to render them, with a GFW dataset endpoint provided.
references.relevance: Shows a public link between the dashboard application and its dataset/layer source system.

references.label: API documentation metadata linkage
references.quote_or_finding: The documentation says each dataset may contain GFW-specific metadata, including info.metadata as the metadata key for the dataset, and applicationConfig.moreInfo can define external links in the legend.
references.relevance: Shows a mechanism for linking displayed layers to metadata and external information, but not exact versioned claim provenance.

references.label: Climate widget formula-to-data linkage
references.quote_or_finding: The climate widget documentation connects above-ground biomass calculations to the whrc_aboveground_biomass_stock_2000__Mg column in summary geotrellis tables and gives an example table UUID.
references.relevance: Provides a concrete partial link from a displayed calculation to an input column/table, though not a full evidence chain.

references.label: Repository branch and release practice
references.quote_or_finding: The README describes develop, master, staging/pre-production/production deployments and GitHub releases to record changes to the app.
references.relevance: Indicates versioning practices for the app, but the evidence does not connect specific releases to specific data and claims.

runs.single_paragraph_summary: The supplied evidence shows that wri/gfw is a public, MIT-licensed Global Forest Watch web application with useful documentation for setup, deployment, data-layer metadata conventions, and several widget calculations. It has clear open-source software practices, CI/testing/security workflows, public issue infrastructure, and public-facing dashboard communication. However, the evidence bundle mostly covers the front-end application rather than the full environmental evidence-production chain: the actual primary datasets, measurement methods, uncertainty/quality controls, backend/API pipelines, exact workflow runs, claim-specific outputs, review records, and versioned claim-to-dataset-code-publication links are largely absent. As a result, the project scores strongest for open-source software and communication, moderately for execution and review, and more weakly for input-data provenance and end-to-end open linkage.
limitations: The assessment uses only the supplied evidence bundle and does not inspect live API responses, GitHub issues, pull requests, releases, package manifests, or the production website beyond the provided excerpts.

The repository appears to be primarily the GFW web app; many datasets, APIs, backend processing systems, satellite products, and model pipelines underlying GFW claims are external to the supplied evidence.
No primary data files, data licences, measurement protocols, quantified uncertainty records, or quality-control documentation were included in the bundle.
No exact dashboard claim, timestamped output, data snapshot, code commit, workflow run, and review/publication record were supplied as a complete traceable chain.

Evidence of community and review processes is limited to repository metadata, CI, pull-request/review-app descriptions, and release practices; substantive review discussions or correction records were not provided.

Publication and communication evidence is limited to the README and documentation files; no formal reports, papers, dashboard version histories, update-cycle documentation, or Creative Commons publication licences were included.
